<Doc1>
Writing
The other day I was walking to class and while following the tangled brick pathways through campus, I merged behind a group of three girls walking together to class laughing and talking about something or another. They were joined by a fourth girl and they all seemed to be having a lovely morning walking and laughing together. I slipped into wondering how my experience might have been different if I had close friends on campus with which to room with, walk to class with, eat in the dining halls with, etc. I lived in an apartment with three very close friends my junior and senior year and that was great, but those first two years of college were pretty lonely. 
Anyhow, just as I found myself trailing off in these thoughts, I happened to see a large hawk perched on the branch of a large oak tree, about level with the top of the two-story building next to it, directly above the path. He turned his head about, seeming to scan the courtyard of students bumbling to class. The pale white feathers of his chest ruffled in the crisp breeze of the morning, while the rest of him seemed to blend with the pale brown tangle of branches behind him, devoid of leaves. He looked so grand up there and I thought about how strange it was that nobody else seemed to notice. Does nobody else look at trees? Don’t get me wrong, I play on my phone walking to class, too, but one would miss so much if they never bothered to look at trees. I feel the same way about looking at the night sky. 
Following this train of thought, I crossed under the bird perched high above and wanted to turn around and look at him from behind to see if his feathers were the same color as the branches, or if he really did have just all white feathers, but I had four minutes to get to class and had to go. I also didn’t want to turn around and face the horde of people walking in the same direction I was trying to get to class. Plus, I sat in the front row and if I was late, I would have to walk in front of all the people in the lecture hall to get to my spot on the front row with my group. I continued scurrying to class. I supposed then, though, that there were times that I missed something fleeting because I, too, was caught up in something else. Or maybe it was the universe telling me to stop feeling sorry for myself for not being as social for a couple years. Or maybe it meant nothing at all—pure coincidence. A hawk in a tree. Minding his business and along comes a woman to extract meaningless theories from a bird catching his morning meal, indifferent and careless of her existence. You can look at one thing in so many ways. 
	My time as an educator was one of the most formative experiences in life. I don’t think anybody, and I mean anybody, could have prepared me for that, not that anyone tried to. I had always thought of teaching as my backup plan if medical school didn’t work out, and later when I became discouraged, a backup plan for if physical therapy school if that didn’t work out. Anyhow, I’ll start from the beginning.
	When COVID-19 first hit I was on an alternative spring break trip in Baytown, North Carolina. It was actually a school trip that I took for a graduation credit with a group called SERVE at STATE UNIVERSITY. We had class once a week to discuss various aspects of volunteer work and changing the world and all that jazz. The class had about sixty people in it split into different groups, each with different alternative spring breaks but all focused on volunteer work. My group had about twelve people in it and our trip was to help with disaster relief after Hurricane Alpha(?) We were to go to the coast and help rebuild houses for people that could not afford the money, time, or labor it took to rebuild on their own. Pretty much every other group focused on bigger picture issues and focused on policy changes within rural, urban, and Latinx communities, which is awesome, but I was always an immediate gratification kind of person. I needed the credit to graduate anyway and it was the last semester of my college career and the only other class I could sign up for to fulfill this credit was something to do with independent research and at the time I had zero interest in research. I toyed with the notion, but decided to give up my spring break since I would also be contributing something positive to someone that needed it, although I would be lying if I said I was ecstatic about it. 
	After each class, we would meet for an hour in our individual groups and over the semester we got to know each other better and I ended up making some acquaintances because each week we had to trade phone numbers with another person and meet up to get to know each other better. Most of us only actually did this for the first couple of weeks, though, because it wasn’t graded and we all seemed to be busy all of the time. The first person I had to trade numbers with was this super tall, tatted, buff guy named Jamal. He towered over me and he always wore Gym Shark clothing and was probably the most in-shape person I have ever met in my life. He would later become a close friend on a spring break trip. I also got to know this guy named Michael, taller than me, super funny and probably the nicest person in the group. He was super warm and inviting and easily the nicest guy in the group. And then there was Chloe. The only thing I really knew about her was that she was blond, pretty, and super chill and pretty much lived on zero sleep and Red Bulls because she worked night shifts at the hospital and went straight to class from there. There were others, but these were the main squad. 
	Anyhow, I didn’t know anyone all that well until the trip and when the day came to leave, we split ourselves into two rental cars, got gas at the Valero outside of Collegeville, and went on our way, listening to the Spotify playlist that everyone contributed to in the weeks leading up to the trip. The ride up was honestly pretty quiet because while we all knew each other’s names, we weren’t exactly close friends.
	After about three hours of driving, we finally arrived to where we would be staying. We were hosted by United Methodist for this spring break, as they have a disaster relief program, and our home for the week was owned by the church. On the outside it was a simple, run-down looking yellow house with cement steps leading up to a wooden porch with about four rocking chairs. We got our things out of the car and headed inside to claim beds. The door opened up to a common area with a table in the center of the room with a couch and some chairs on the left side of the room, a box television on the right that we didn’t turn on for the entire trip, and a desk in the right corner of the room. Directly opposite the front door was an entryway into a room that, for lack of better wording, just led into other rooms. It was like a hallway, but square? Anyhow, as you walked into the entryway, there was a small breakfast table shoved into the corner immediately to the right and a large china cabinet on the left. Before the china cabinet was a hall that lead to a room with four bunk beds and a bathroom. After the china cabinet was another hallway which lead to a room with 4 sets of bunk beds, one of which I claimed to be mine because it was the least-grungy-looking room with the most natural light. Directly opposite this entryway was the entryway into the small kitchen which led to a small storage area on the left and the back door, where we found aluminum cans of Annheiser-Busch water—not beer, water. After Hurricane Alpha(?), they stopped canning beer and started canning and sending pallets of water to the victims the category four storm left littered behind. To the right past the breakfast table was another hallway that lead to the main bathroom, and then a hallway that curved back to the right towards the common area and at the end of that hallway, across from a secondary entrance to the common area, was a room with two bunk beds where most of the guys slept. The place wasn’t gross, just bare bones and outdated. 
	Our schedule for the week was pretty booked. We spent most of the weekday mornings rebuilding a middle-aged lady’s trailer. I think I expected there to be lots of other people rebuilding, too. United Methodist, our host for the trip is a church franchise with a church in almost every decent sized rural town in the south. Only two people outside of our group were present at the build site.
The first was a medium-build, aging, man with bland off-white hair with a mustache to match. He was super friendly, albeit a bit retro in his views and mannerisms, but he was overjoyed to welcome us to their abode. You could tell he was passionate about what he was doing. The other person was a softly aging woman with a faded tan, ashy blonde hair, and wrinkles that appeared to be from many days and nights of smiling and laughing with friends. She was kind, too, but she only came out to the work site a couple times to observe. I don’t entirely remember what her role in everything was.
We only actually worked on one lady’s trailer that was destroyed by the storm. On the first day, we got a safety briefing about some of the tools and when we were required to wear protective glasses, suits, gloves. It ended with David informing us that there were only two pairs of safety glasses. For eleven people. We then assembled ourselves into groups for different projects: installing insulation underneath the house; cutting, putting up and tacking down vinyl skirting; flooring. David said we weren’t skilled enough to do drywall. He was pretty good at assuming things without asking any questions. I’m so far from a professional drywaller it isn’t funny, but I have helped my parents several times with doing our own. I spent many months at one point watching them do it on weekends alongside a small construction team doing other various things. 
I opted for vinyl siding duty along with Nina, Sophie, and Liv. No one really wanted to go under the house, not because they were preppy college kids or anything, but it had a corrosive and slimy appearance and honestly looked kind of sketchy. Nevertheless, four people stepped up: Chloe, Raj, Amit, and Brian. Then, there was Michael, Jamal, Emma, Megan spread amongst other jobs. On other days that week, some of us did flooring and cleaned up a pile of construction debris piled as high as the porch landing. David stepped in occasionally to tell us how to use something, but he never really helped. I don’t blame him, I’m sure it’s a big job to make sure everything is done right, but he hovered, and it was kind of awkward. That combined with his lack of help caused some of us to look at him a little differently, but it was whatever. 
Halfway through, we ate the lunches we had prepared and packed for ourselves in the small, dimly lit, kitchen that morning. We sat around and talked and I think I remember a day where a few of us were trying to do cartwheels. One day we sat in the field behind the trailer and picked grass and randomly dispersed clover flowers and laughed and looked up at the blue sky with its fluffy bright white clouds. We also used this time to drive a couple miles down the road to some seemingly affiliated facility—a small building tucked into the corner of a parking lot, where we were allowed to use the bathrooms in the burgundy-carpeted front lobby. Sometimes we went to a BP a couple miles in the other direction, instead so we could grab extra snacks at lunch. We went other times during the day of course if we really had to go. 
One lunch in particular sticks out to me because of something David said. Some of us were sitting at a sun-bleached wooden picnic table with shrunken boards from years of exposure to the elements. I wonder if it was put there by our hosts or for us or if its weathering frame steadily withstood the hurricane’s forces. I sat in the middle of one bench with a couple of other people. Chloe sat diagonally to my right on the other side of the table next to David, who was on the end. Somehow, David slipped the conversation into fossil fuels and how they were better for the environment than wind turbines. He proceeded to to tell us that “wind turbines were the number one cause of death for bald eagles.” Most of the faces around the table reflected the dialup noises going off in our head as we sat silently. Bald eagles nest mostly in large trees in large forests. 
When we were not helping rebuild, we were visiting different parts of Baytown. Some of the things aligned with our reason for being in Baytown, but some were bent into shape somewhat unwillingly. Visits to the fire department, the water processing facility, and a maritime museum were nestled in between nights of cooking with our pre-assigned partners and talks around the table about our activities and what we were gaining from the experience. 
The visit to the fire department definitely made sense because the firefighters were on the front lines for evacuating people before the hurricane and helping them after. When we arrived to the fire department we were upstairs into a conference room with rectangle tables forming a U-shape that faced the front of the room. Up front sat the fire chief and a couple of other staff. Someone would ask a question and they would answer. Some of it was super interesting, as they told us about people refusing to leave their homes behind and how they had to tell them that nobody would be coming for them during the storm. They also talked about how after the storm, the community was a big part of the recovery and rebuilding process; it wasn’t just professionals, but mainly normal people with boats and resources helping their neighbors. Not long into this Q&A session, a man with dark colored hair and a shaven face sauntered in. The mood of our hosts up front immediately shifted. At some point he was introduced, or maybe he introduced himself, as the chief’s son. As the session went on, he would interrupt to answer questions and it became quite obvious that the other staff, his dad included, didn’t seem to like him too much. I immediately didn’t like him. It was something about the way he presented himself, so arrogant while likely very subpar. 
By the end of the session, he had all but taken over the answering of questions. He then offered to show us a room downstairs where they educated children on fire safety. He led us back downstairs and into a room with brightly colored walls and little tables and chairs. Somewhere in there, or maybe just outside of the room, were pictures of people dressed up as clowns, their mascot for fire safety, apparently. The chief’s son proudly explained that he had been the clown for a little while, educating kids on fire safety. Don’t get me wrong, teaching kids about fire safety is super duper important, but he was just a little too proud of it. We didn’t stay in there long, because he then led us out into the firetruck bays and at this point the rest of the staff basically let him have us. 
In there, he told us all a little about the firetrucks and equipment and such. I stayed at the back of the group and didn’t pay much attention, though, because I had helped Robert do equipment checks on the trucks at Riverdale and Oak Grove Fire Departments countless times and I even volunteered there for a couple years once I was old enough. Furthermore, Robert was on the fire department in Springfield for as long as I could remember, so I grew up around it and pretty much knew everything he was telling the group about. 
But then the absolute worst part was that he had us all gathered around and began telling stories about him being a hero. To recount this is super painful because of just how horribly cringy it was because if you’ve ever been around people that actually save people, they don’t talk about it the way he did. He told a few very dramatic stories about fire calls he had been on and how he was the first one on scene, which is super suspicious in itself because there were several like that and they were all structure fires, which really aren’t that common in comparison to other calls you get. Anyhow, in one of these stories he recounted how he was at the station, the alarm bell rang, and he quickly grabbed his gear and hopped in a truck and went straight there—first on scene, of course. He arrive to the house engulfed in flames. He jumped out and barged in there and trekked his way through all the smoke and fire and soot looking for the old lady that was supposed to be living there. He included lots of little fine details that I honestly cannot remember anymore because I was sure most of it was mispresented, but he kept this prideful, heroic, and ultimately ungenuine tone throughout his story. And at one point, he went straight into choking up and looked down at the ground as he raised his hand to his face. He apologized for getting choked up and I think he was actively trying to push out some tears. This was the fakest shit I had ever seen. And amazingly, some of the people in our group were eating that shit up. I had to keep myself from busting out laughing because was this guy serious? But alas, he found the old lady and saved the day and was a hero. The reaction of the rest of the staff to him, his cadence, his tone, his attitude, the way he told the story, all contributed to him coming across as a complete sociopath and I was not the only one. Luckily, Michael was in the back of the group with me snapping pictures, as he is a photographer, and we mouthed to each other a few times “Is he serious?” and “What the fuck?”
After the tour and story time, we all piled back into our respective two vehicles. In our vehicle was myself, Chloe, Michael, Jamal, and Nina. As soon as we got back into the van, I let loose, “That guy definitely set all those fires” I said. Nina was shocked but then everyone else agreed with me to some extent or another, or at least agreed that he was super fucking weird and was lying about a few details. 
Sometimes it feels like I’m running in place. I am going to school and trying to advance and I’m making progress and all that good stuff. But, it’s the same thing all the time. A scheduled routine of class and work and trying to squeeze in time for family and friends and time to rest. But I want to experience everything life has to offer. Sometimes I feel like I get bored with a job once I figure it out and experience and live it for a little while. But then, I want to experience something else. I’ve long had a goal of going to medical school and that’s what I decided to do once I entered college. But, then it quickly changed. Introduction biology and chemistry were much harder than expected. I never had to study. Just pay attention, do the assignments, take the test, make A’s. I made a few bad grades here and there, but I honestly don’t remember studying much. Anyway, I shifted to physical therapy and changed my major from Biology to Exercise and Sport Science, because I thought Biology 101 would be much more about the human body, but it wasn’t and Exercise and Sport Science was. Ironic, because I’ve never been the athletic type. I did softball for a while, but wasn’t that good. I ran track and did really good the first meet, but I was just there to stay in shape so I didn’t really try. I wasn’t even that good at cheerleading, but I did okay. But, EXSS was so much more involved with anatomy and physiology. Anyway, I focused on becoming a physical therapy, although looking back I think I must have felt that it was a boring choice for me. I shadowed a physical therapist for 2 weeks and worked in a private clinic as a receptionist for a while, and I knew how boring it looked. Although, they were both private clinics, so I suppose I could have branched out more, but I took the opportunities I had received. 
Anyhow, when COVID hit, everything stopped and we couldn’t do anything. I lost all three of my jobs—the physical therapy job, a job at Slice Pizzeria, and my work-study job on campus as a Safety Equipment Monitor (which is an absurdly big mouthful to say out loud). Then, I believe I saw my way out. I lost all of my jobs and couldn’t find anything else due to everything shutting down; virtual jobs would not work for me because after everything started shutting down, I moved out of my apartment and into Kevin’s parents’ house, where the wifi was less than ideal. Looking back, the jobs were an odd combination, but I loved that I got to experience every single one of them. 
Then, a few months into lockdown, an opportunity for a position to be a teacher came up. I took it, was there for three years, the longest I’ve ever been at a job. I loved it, but it was emotionally draining, and it took a chunk out of me, I think. I was so anxious and mortified every day that something would go wrong and who the hell put me in charge of 60 kids every day? It was not my forte at all, and I think I knew that halfway through my second year, but it was a good paying job with benefits and I actually did love connecting with students. There were some tough ones, but each had their own story, many of them heartbreaking. I got the opportunity to see this space and time through the lenses of so many kids. I often felt I was more a therapist, than a teacher, but I didn’t mind it. I do feel that it shaped me, and I’m so glad I got the opportunity to form the connections I did and experience it all. Plus, I’m a licensed teacher, which is kind of awesome! 
But, I needed to move on. It was getting to be too much, and I decided I wanted to go back to medical school. So, here I am. Taking classes. Progressing with the feeling of running in place. But I do not want to feel like I am running in place. I want to experience. I still want to become a doctor, but I want to experience things. I want to be outside. I want to live. I want to experience as much as I possibly can for the short slice of time we get out of an eternity, because I know that there is never enough time to finish it all. There’s so much out there, but we keep doing the same thing day after day, week after week. The same shitty bar every week (which I do love, but you get my point). The same barrage of bullshit ranging bills that spring up when it’s least convenient, trying and failing at saving money for the future because of said bills, not having enough time to do anything other than recuperate from the weight that the week has put on our backs. I want to break out of that cycle. I want to do things. It doesn’t have to be big, new things all the time, even things I’ve already done like kayaking or walking through the woods or trying a new coffee shop or something. Something. There’s so much to do, and I want to do it all. 
Strange Dreams
	I feel as though I’ve always had strange dreams, but then again, I guess all dreams are at least a little strange. Even when I’ve had a dream where nothing extraordinary happens, when it’s like living some version of a mundane day with no flying elephants or floors that fall from beneath your feet or anything like that, even then it seems strange that I should be dreaming of walking to and from class and chatting with my former roommate about my weekend plans when I could be dreaming about so much more. Anyhow, I feel the need to write down some of my stranger dreams, because some of them bewilder me and have such a pull on me that it seems important that there is some tangible proof of it outside of my head and the words spoken to others about them. 
Sometimes I think there is more to them, that they are three-dimensional in a way that not everyone understands. I feel like most people see them as two-dimensional, a flat picture show on the back of their eyelids that is over when their morning alarm abruptly interrupts it. The depth with which I feel some people perceive their dreams is comparable to a pool covered by a pool cover. When you go to sleep, you jump onto the pool cover and you’ll get wet, you’ll dream, but that two-dimensional tarp covering only allows you to move so deep into the pool and into the full realm of your dream. But what if there is more depth to the act of dreaming? What if you can punch through the tarp and actually be submerged in its hold? I know there are a good number of people that think about dreams this way, as conversations surrounding dream walking and the like that have been around for centuries, but to actually think about it and what it might mean is terrifying. 
	One of the earliest dreams I recall that really got me thinking more deeply about dreams was when I was around 10 or maybe 11. I remember that it was myself and my classmates and it was like we were on a field trip, except we were touring this old house that had the feel of a farmhouse with lightbulbs hanging from the ceiling by slowly swinging cords that lit the rooms very poorly. I don’t remember entering the house, I just remember being there and how eerie and dark it felt. The first place I remember us seeing was the kitchen. We peered into the kitchen from an entryway that separated it from the living area that we were standing in. A bright white bulb hung above the kitchen sink, highlighting the dinginess of the kitchen—every little speck of dirt and grime on the white porcelain sink and the laminated tile floors was exposed. I remember it making me feel uneasy. We then ventured in a line down a long, dark hallway that was only lit from the light coming from the rooms connected to it. I felt so uneasy being there, but my classmates seemed overly comfortable there and ssort of split off into these rooms, in no particular order, and seemed to be exploring freely. I was toward the back of the line and I came to a room on the left and looked in. There were maybe four or five kids in there, and one of them was sitting on the floor with their legs and feet stretched open like you would to stretch for gym class. Next to him, was a slightly larger dark shadow that mirrored the kid’s sitting stance and the shadow’s foot overlapped with the kid’s. I screamed and pointed in horror and my teacher who was standing in the hallway put her hand on my shoulder and asked me what was wrong and I tried to explain, as I looked back I realized the shadow had disappeared. I didn’t want to look ridiculous, so I just brushed it off.	
	Our little tour continued down the hallway and out of a side door that led us outside. We exited into the side yard, where there was a graveyard. It was a cloudy, grim day with a comfortable temperature, but the atmosphere was disturbing. One would think the graveyard would be the obvious main focus, but I was closely examining the house. Next to the door we had exited through, there was a rounded window that jutted out of the house, like one that would be for a breakfast nook or a round window seat. I remember each small pane of glass was framed with molding covered by peeling white paint. Each small pane came together to make this three-dimensional, rounded appendage that jutted out from the house. There may have been a breakfast nook or a round window seat nestled in it, but I didn’t know because I wasn’t focused on that. I noticed fingerprints on the outside of the windows and as I brought my face closer to inspect them, I noticed that the fingerprints were raised, almost like someone had touched the glass with tar on their fingertips. I reached my own fingers up to touch them, to see if they really were raised, I think, and I was sucked away from the scene with my classmates. There was a sudden rushing of noise and images that I can describe as agony. It was the sound of girls screaming, or perhaps one girl screaming a lot, in such torment. The image that accompanied the screams was a blur of a girl with long, black hair holding her head in her hands and shaking it back and forth as if screaming, but the sounds and the vision were disembodied from each other. They certainly went together, but they weren’t synced up. It was chaotic and disorienting. It was over in a flash, but the wailing of the girl embodied an eternity of pain and anguish, and it felt like it lasted at least an hour. I came back to where I was before alongside my classmates in the side-yard-graveyard of this creepy ass house. It was soon after this that I woke up. 
	Some of the fine details of this dream have faded from my memory over time, but at the time I could recount every little detail. I could close my eyes and see it all over again. That morning, I woke up and Jessica soon after. We were sitting in the living room floor—maybe we had slept on a pallet, but I don’t remember for sure anymore, but I began telling her that I had this really weird dream. I began telling her about how I was on a field trip in this house and I began describing the kitchen and she abruptly stopped me and said she was in a house in her dream, too, and the kitchen looked just like that. This struck me as bizarre, so before I continued, I asked her what the rest of the layout of the house was like. I became cold in my skin as she methodically described the layout of the house exactly down to the hallway, the order of the rooms, and what was in each room. At a couple points, I interrupted her to add in a small detail like the placement of a light or a bookshelf, and she excitedly agreed that it was the same in her dream too. Her dream was more light than mine, though. It was a sunny day in her dream and the house wasn’t exactly scary to her, a stark juxtaposition to the overcast, foreboding day that hosted the haunt-infested house that I visited in my nightmare. I was glad her dream wasn’t like mine, because as mild as it is in comparison to other nightmares I’ve had since, my dream scared me to my core. 
I thought about it for days and maybe even weeks, as I pondered what it meant and why I had felt it so deeply and how the hell we both dreamed about the same exact house on the same exact night—a house mind you, that neither of us had ever seen or ever stepped foot in and didn’t even know it to exist. Every so often I find myself thinking of how to find out if a house like that one exists. If it did exist, I wonder if I’d feel anything if I walked inside. There is a house in Mapleton that faintly reminds me of it, but it just isn’t quite right. I can never stop thinking about how strange it is that we should dream of the same house with the same layout that may not even exist. Why did we dream of the same house? How did we dream of the same house? If it were a big coincidence, how were even the smallest details the same? How were we able to confirm these details with each other by taking turns imparting them? I don’t know that it means anything, but I can not believe that we it happened coincidentally—not to that level of detail. 
 I don’t even know what dreams to write about next. I’ve had so many lately that bother me. And they’re all so detailed that I know it will take so much time to do them justice and to really take you there with me. The details of dreams also fade so fast that I don’t know if I can put you there with me with the now fewer details that are singed into my mind. I’ll try. 
	Over the last several weeks (I’ve honestly lost count at this point), I’ve been having these hyper realistic dreams. It feels like I’ve punched through the tarp pool cover and am submerged in them, feeling them, really living them. I wake up unrested because I’ve been living in my mind, meticulously making my way through each and every minute of the day, or even days, that I live out in my dreams. 
	I suppose I will start with the dream that began this streak of unrestful sleep. The beginning of the dream has faded from my mind at this point, but it is dark out and I am at this large log cabin that I recognize from previous dreams. Little Sierra, Jasmine, Maya, and I are walking toward another smaller, but still full-sized log cabin about 75 yards away from the main house. It feels soft and pleasant outside. The walkway between the two houses is unlit, but the soft glowing light from both houses is enough that we can see our way there. Connecting the two houses is a worn path in tall, knee-high grass that sways in the night breeze. We are going to this smaller cabin to hang out and have a sleepover. Maya is running around and cracking jokes and we are all laughing as we make our way up to the cabin. I feel at peace. 
As we arrive to the front of the cabin, we walk to the right side where there is a brown, waist-high wooden picket fence that surrounds a small portion of the right-side yard, which has a tree roughly placed in the middle. We open the little gate to go through and into the house. Abruptly, a man materializes from the splotchy shadows that are being created by the house’s soft glowing light that filters through the orangey leaves of the tree. The light illuminates his white skin in patches, but in such a way that makes his whole face visible. He has dark brown hair and is somewhat attractive, but his mouth slowly curves up into a menacing smile that sharply contradicts the delicate light on his face and he walks boldly toward us. It all happens so fast and he attacks Maya and the next thing I know she is on the ground on her back, head turned to the side, eyes open, staring out towards that soft, swaying grass, but there is nothing behind them. 
I turn and lunge at the guy, tackling him to the ground but I notice someone else lying face down on the ground just off into the shadow of the tree, though I cannot make out who it is. I do know I don’t see Little Sierra around, and I am hopeful that she had time to get away. I do everything I can to pin this man down so he cannot hurt anyone else, especially not Sierra. I try to pin his limbs to the ground with mine, but he is wriggling beneath me and is a bit bigger than me, so I start hitting him. I am expending all the energy I have in my body. I cannot let him get to anyone else. I am crying and grappling anything I can get a hold of to hurt him and send him into an eternal sleep. I can’t let him hurt anyone else. And then, finally, he disappears. I can’t believe it, this has never happened to me in a dream before; typically, all of my efforts are laughed off by my assailant as they overpower me. I get up onto my feet, crying but relieved that it is over and relieved that I was finally able to defend myself. But I look around and my slain companions were no longer on the ground. ### Theme 1: The Longing for Authentic Connection Amidst Isolation

This theme explores the fundamental human need for genuine relationships and the pain of loneliness, neglect, and betrayal that arises when that need goes unmet. It manifests as a persistent search for community and a fear of being alone.

### 1. The Nature of Friendship: Deep Longing vs. Casual Acquaintances
